intro: Hi! In Indonesian, banyak and sedikit work for everything. In English you choose: many, much or a lot of, a few or a little, too much or too many. Warm-up: is there a lot of traffic in your city?
teachingNotes: The Indonesian trap: 'banyak' covers many, much and a lot of; 'sedikit' covers a few and a little; 'terlalu banyak' covers too much and too many. The English word depends on the noun: plural countable (cars, people, eggs) or uncountable (money, water, rice). Learners know countable/uncountable, some/any and How much/How many from a1-countable-some-any; build on it, and remind them that people/children are plural countable nouns without -s. Common error: *'How much people …?' → How many people …?

many + plural countable, much + uncountable, a lot of + both. In positive sentences say 'a lot of' (Rina has a lot of friends; There is a lot of rice). 'much' alone in a positive sentence sounds strange (*'I have much money'): use it in questions and negatives (Do you have much time? I don't have much money). 'many' is fine in all three, but in everyday positive sentences 'a lot of' is more natural. 'too much' and 'so much' are normal in positive sentences: say why if the learner asks. The verb follows the noun after a lot of: There IS a lot of traffic, There ARE a lot of cars. 'lots of' = a lot of, a bit more informal; accept it. Short answers 'Yes, a lot.' / 'No, not much.' are fine.

Words to remember (uncountable in English, though Indonesian thinking counts them): money, information, advice, furniture, traffic (also homework, luggage if asked). No a/an, no -s, use much/a little/too much: How much information? a little advice, too much furniture. To count them, count something else: rupiah or notes for money, chairs and tables for furniture, cars for traffic, or 'a piece of' for information and advice. Don't call *'informations' or *'advices' a small slip: they are very common mistakes for Indonesian speakers.

a few + plural countable (a few eggs, a few friends); a little + uncountable (a little sugar, a little time). Common error: *'I have a few money' → I have a little money. Both mean 'some, not many, and that's OK'. 'few' / 'little' WITHOUT 'a' mean 'not enough' (Few people come here. I have little time.); mention it only as a note, don't test it. Don't teach 'a bit of' unless asked (it means a little, and is common in British English).

too much + uncountable, too many + plural countable: too much salt, too many cars. Common error: *'There are too much cars in Jakarta' → too many cars. 'too' means more than you want, a problem; 'a lot of' is neutral (a lot of friends is good, too many people on the bus is a problem). Don't teach 'too + adjective' (too hot), 'enough', 'not enough', no/none or comparatives here.

Limits: present tenses only (simple present, present continuous, there is/are, have/have got, can, I'd like, imperatives). No past simple (the node's commonError 'How much people came?' is only a model), no will, no present perfect. Real contexts: Jakarta traffic, warung, pasar, kantor, kos, angkot, ojek, prices in rupiah.

keyPoints.title: much, many and a lot of
keyPoints.explanation: Indonesian banyak has three English words. many + plural countable nouns (cars, people); much + uncountable nouns (money, water); a lot of + both. In positive sentences use a lot of; use much in questions and negatives. Money, information, advice, furniture and traffic are uncountable: much, not many, and no -s.

examples.en: There are a lot of cars on this road.
examples.id: Ada banyak mobil di jalan ini.

examples.en: How many students are in your class?

id.title: much, many dan a lot of
id.explanation: Kata banyak dalam bahasa Indonesia punya tiga kata dalam bahasa Inggris. many + kata benda jamak yang bisa dihitung (cars, people); much + kata benda yang tidak bisa dihitung (money, water); a lot of + keduanya. Di kalimat positif pakai a lot of; pakai much di pertanyaan dan kalimat negatif. Money, information, advice, furniture dan traffic tidak bisa dihitung: pakai much, bukan many, dan tanpa -s.

keyPoints.title: a few and a little
keyPoints.explanation: Indonesian sedikit has two English words. a few + plural countable nouns (a few friends); a little + uncountable nouns (a little money). Both mean 'not many / not much, but some'. Not 'a few money'.

examples.en: I have a few friends in Surabaya.
examples.id: Saya punya beberapa teman di Surabaya.

examples.en: Add a little water to the rice.

id.title: a few dan a little
id.explanation: Kata sedikit dalam bahasa Indonesia punya dua kata dalam bahasa Inggris. a few + kata benda jamak yang bisa dihitung (a few friends); a little + kata benda yang tidak bisa dihitung (a little money). Keduanya berarti 'tidak banyak, tapi ada'. Bukan 'a few money'.

keyPoints.title: too much and too many
keyPoints.explanation: too much / too many = terlalu banyak: more than you want, a problem. too many + plural countable nouns; too much + uncountable nouns. Not 'too much cars'.

examples.en: There are too many people on this bus.
examples.id: Terlalu banyak orang di bus ini.

id.title: too much dan too many
id.explanation: too much / too many = terlalu banyak: lebih dari yang kamu mau, jadi masalah. too many + kata benda jamak yang bisa dihitung; too much + kata benda yang tidak bisa dihitung. Bukan 'too much cars'.

material.title: Banyak: many, much or a lot of?

blocks.text:
Indonesian has one word, **banyak**: *banyak mobil, banyak uang*. English has three, and the **noun** after it decides (a noun = the name of a thing: *car, money*):
- **many** + a **plural countable** noun (things you count one by one, with -s): many cars, many eggs. Also **people** and **children**: plurals without -s, but countable.
- **much** + an **uncountable** noun (things you don't count one by one, no -s): much water, much money.
- **a lot of** + **both**: a lot of cars, a lot of money. It's the easy, safe choice.

There's one more rule: **where** in the sentence. In a **positive** sentence (no *not*, not a question), say **a lot of**: *I have a lot of money*, not *I have much money* (much alone sounds strange there). Use **much** in **questions** and **negatives** (sentences with *not*): *Do you have much money? I don't have much money.* **many** is fine everywhere, but in everyday positive sentences **a lot of** sounds more natural.

id.text:
Bahasa Indonesia punya satu kata, **banyak**: *banyak mobil, banyak uang*. Bahasa Inggris punya tiga, dan **kata benda** sesudahnya yang menentukan (kata benda = nama benda: *car, money*):
- **many** + kata benda **jamak yang bisa dihitung** (benda yang dihitung satu per satu, pakai -s): many cars, many eggs. Juga **people** dan **children**: bentuk jamak tanpa -s, tapi tetap bisa dihitung.
- **much** + kata benda **yang tidak bisa dihitung** (uncountable, tidak dihitung satu per satu, tanpa -s): much water, much money.
- **a lot of** + **keduanya**: a lot of cars, a lot of money. Ini pilihan yang paling gampang dan aman.

Ada satu aturan lagi: **di kalimat apa**. Di kalimat **positif** (tanpa *not*, bukan pertanyaan), pakai **a lot of**: *I have a lot of money*, bukan *I have much money* (much sendirian terdengar aneh di situ). Pakai **much** di **pertanyaan** dan kalimat **negatif** (kalimat dengan *not*): *Do you have much money? I don't have much money.* **many** boleh di mana saja, tapi di kalimat positif sehari-hari **a lot of** terdengar lebih alami.

rows.en: There are a lot of tourists in Bali.
Pak Hasan has a lot of money.
There aren't many shops in my village.
rows.id: Tidak banyak toko di desa saya.

rows.en: I don't have much time today.
rows.id: Saya tidak punya banyak waktu hari ini.

rows.en: How many children do they have?
Do you have much homework? — No, not much.

id.note: pertanyaan + tidak bisa dihitung; jawaban singkat

blocks.text: After **a lot of**, the verb follows the noun: There **is** a lot of rice (uncountable → is). There **are** a lot of people (plural → are). And Indonesian *berapa* still splits in two, as you know: not 'How much people?' but **How many people?** You'll also hear **lots of**: it means the same as a lot of, a bit more casual.

id.text: Sesudah **a lot of**, kata kerjanya mengikuti kata bendanya: There **is** a lot of rice (tidak bisa dihitung → is). There **are** a lot of people (jamak → are). Dan *berapa* tetap terbagi dua, seperti yang sudah kamu tahu: bukan 'How much people?' tapi **How many people?** Kamu juga akan mendengar **lots of**: artinya sama dengan a lot of, sedikit lebih santai.

blocks.explain: It's a positive sentence, so a lot of is the natural choice. much is for uncountable nouns (shoes is plural), and a lot needs of before a noun.

id.explain: Ini kalimat positif, jadi a lot of yang paling alami. much untuk kata benda yang tidak bisa dihitung (shoes itu jamak), dan a lot perlu of sebelum kata benda.

id.title: Banyak: many, much atau a lot of?

material.title: Words to remember: money, information, advice, furniture, traffic

blocks.text:
Some words feel countable in Indonesian, but in English they are **uncountable**: **no a/an, no -s**, and they take **much, a little, too much** (not *many, a few, too many*). This is an exception list: learn these five by heart.
- **money** (uang): you count the **rupiah** or the notes, not the money. *How much money?*
- **information** (informasi): Indonesian says *informasi-informasi*, but English never says 'informations'.
- **advice** (saran, nasihat): not 'an advice' or 'advices'. To count it, say **a piece of advice**.
- **furniture** (perabot, mebel): English sees it as one group. Count the things: *two chairs and a table*.
- **traffic** (lalu lintas): it's the whole flow on the road. Count the **cars** or **motorbikes**, not the traffic.

id.text:
Ada kata yang terasa bisa dihitung dalam bahasa Indonesia, tapi dalam bahasa Inggris **tidak bisa dihitung**: **tanpa a/an, tanpa -s**, dan memakai **much, a little, too much** (bukan *many, a few, too many*). Ini daftar pengecualian: hafalkan lima kata ini.
- **money** (uang): yang dihitung **rupiah**-nya atau lembarannya, bukan uangnya. *How much money?*
- **information** (informasi): bahasa Indonesia bilang *informasi-informasi*, tapi bahasa Inggris tidak pernah bilang 'informations'.
- **advice** (saran, nasihat): bukan 'an advice' atau 'advices'. Untuk menghitungnya, bilang **a piece of advice** (satu saran).
- **furniture** (perabot, mebel): bahasa Inggris melihatnya sebagai satu kelompok. Hitung bendanya: *two chairs and a table*.
- **traffic** (lalu lintas): ini seluruh arus di jalan. Hitung **mobil** atau **motor**-nya, bukan traffic-nya.

rows.en: How much money do you need for the trip?
rows.id: Kamu butuh berapa banyak uang untuk perjalanan itu?

rows.en: The website has a lot of information about the trains.
rows.id: Situs itu punya banyak informasi tentang kereta.

rows.en: My mother gives me a lot of advice.
rows.id: Ibu saya memberi saya banyak nasihat.

rows.en: There isn't much furniture in my room at the kos.
rows.id: Tidak banyak perabot di kamar kos saya.

rows.en: There is a lot of traffic in Bandung on Sundays.
rows.id: Lalu lintas di Bandung ramai sekali setiap hari Minggu.

blocks.text: Want to count information or advice? Use **a piece of**: *a piece of information, two pieces of advice*. The word **piece** is countable, so it takes -s. Two more words like these that you'll meet: **homework** (PR) and **luggage** (bagasi, koper).

id.text: Mau menghitung information atau advice? Pakai **a piece of**: *a piece of information, two pieces of advice*. Kata **piece** bisa dihitung, jadi memakai -s. Dua kata lain seperti ini yang akan kamu temui: **homework** (PR) dan **luggage** (bagasi, koper).

options: Can you give me an advice?

Can you give me some advice?
blocks.explain: advice is uncountable in English: no an, no -s. Some advice is correct (or a piece of advice).

id.explain: advice tidak bisa dihitung dalam bahasa Inggris: tanpa an, tanpa -s. Some advice yang benar (atau a piece of advice).

material.title: Sedikit: a few or a little?

blocks.text:
**Sedikit** also has two English words. Again, the noun decides:
- **a few** + a **plural countable** noun: *a few eggs, a few friends, a few minutes*.
- **a little** + an **uncountable** noun: *a little rice, a little money, a little time*.

Both mean 'not many / not much, but there is some, and that's OK'. So not 'a few money': money is uncountable, so it's **a little money**.

id.text:
**Sedikit** juga punya dua kata dalam bahasa Inggris. Lagi-lagi, kata bendanya yang menentukan:
- **a few** + kata benda **jamak yang bisa dihitung**: *a few eggs, a few friends, a few minutes*.
- **a little** + kata benda **yang tidak bisa dihitung**: *a little rice, a little money, a little time*.

Keduanya berarti 'tidak banyak, tapi ada, dan itu tidak masalah'. Jadi bukan 'a few money': money tidak bisa dihitung, jadi **a little money**.

rows.en: There are a few chairs in the meeting room.
rows.id: Ada beberapa kursi di ruang rapat.

rows.note: a language is uncountable → a little

id.note: bahasa tidak bisa dihitung → a little

rows.en: Put a little oil in the pan.

id.note: oil: tidak bisa dihitung → a little

blocks.text: Careful with **a**. Without it, **few** and **little** mean 'not enough' (*hampir tidak ada*): *Few people come to this shop* (sepi, bad for the shop). *I have little time* (saya hampir tidak punya waktu). With **a**, the feeling is positive: *a few people come* (ada beberapa). For now, use **a few** and **a little**.

id.text: Hati-hati dengan **a**. Tanpa a, **few** dan **little** berarti 'tidak cukup' (hampir tidak ada): *Few people come to this shop* (sepi, tidak bagus untuk tokonya). *I have little time* (saya hampir tidak punya waktu). Dengan **a**, rasanya positif: *a few people come* (ada beberapa). Untuk sekarang, pakai **a few** dan **a little** saja.

blocks.prompt: Can I have ___ rice, please? Just half a plate.
blocks.explain: rice is uncountable, so a little rice. a few is for plural nouns, like a few eggs.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: Can I have ___ rice, please? Just half a plate.
id.explain: rice tidak bisa dihitung, jadi a little rice. a few untuk kata benda jamak, seperti a few eggs.

material.title: Terlalu banyak: too much or too many?

blocks.text:
**too** means 'more than you want': it's a **problem** (*terlalu*). Same rule as before:
- **too many** + a **plural countable** noun: *too many cars, too many people*.
- **too much** + an **uncountable** noun: *too much salt, too much noise, too much homework*.

Compare: **a lot of** is neutral (*banyak*): *I have a lot of friends* (nice!). **too many** is a complaint (*terlalu banyak*): *There are too many people on this bus* (I can't sit down!).

Wait: much in a positive sentence? Yes: **much** alone sounds strange there, but **too much** is normal in every kind of sentence.

id.text:
**too** berarti 'lebih dari yang kamu mau': ini **masalah** (*terlalu*). Aturannya sama seperti tadi:
- **too many** + kata benda **jamak yang bisa dihitung**: *too many cars, too many people*.
- **too much** + kata benda **yang tidak bisa dihitung**: *too much salt, too much noise, too much homework*.

Bandingkan: **a lot of** itu netral (*banyak*): *I have a lot of friends* (asyik!). **too many** itu keluhan (*terlalu banyak*): *There are too many people on this bus* (saya tidak dapat tempat duduk!).

Lho, much di kalimat positif? Ya: **much** sendirian terdengar aneh di sana, tapi **too much** normal di kalimat apa saja.

rows.en: There are too many cars in Jakarta.
I can't study. There's too much noise.
rows.id: Saya tidak bisa belajar. Terlalu berisik.

rows.en: Dimas has too many meetings today.
rows.id: Dimas punya terlalu banyak rapat hari ini.

rows.en: My son spends too much money on games.
rows.id: Anak saya menghabiskan terlalu banyak uang untuk game.

blocks.text: Don't use **too** when you just mean 'very many'. *Bali has a lot of beautiful beaches* is a compliment. *Bali has too many beaches* sounds like a complaint!

id.text: Jangan pakai **too** kalau maksudmu hanya 'banyak sekali'. *Bali has a lot of beautiful beaches* itu pujian. *Bali has too many beaches* terdengar seperti keluhan!
